rejected.title: Women and the war
card: Women could not serve as soldiers in the First World War. Many Australian women found other ways to take part.
Overseas
Women served as nurses with the Australian Army Nursing Service. They worked in hospitals and casualty clearing stations near the fighting, and on hospital ships.
At home
Women raised money, knitted socks and packed parcels of supplies for soldiers. Many joined groups such as the Red Cross to do this work.
Conscription
Women also took part in the conscription debate. Some campaigned for conscription, and others campaigned against it. They did not share one view.
rejected.remember: Women backed the war effort in many ways, but they did not all agree about conscription.

a.q: Which statement best describes how Australian women took part in the First World War?
opts: They nursed and knitted, and differed on conscription
They fought as soldiers and led the home campaigns
They stayed out of the war effort and public debate
They knitted and nursed, and all backed conscription
a.why: Women nursed overseas, knitted and packed supplies at home, and joined the conscription debate on both sides. The option saying they all backed conscription is wrong because some women campaigned against it.
a.clue: Think about both their jobs and their opinions.

b.q: In 1917, Edith in Adelaide knits socks for soldiers and speaks at a rally against conscription. Her neighbour Joan packs parcels and speaks at a rally for it. What does this show?
opts: Women who backed the war effort could differ on conscription
Women who helped soldiers all wanted conscription introduced
Women who knitted socks were all against conscription
Women who spoke at rallies were doing so as army nurses
b.why: Both women helped soldiers, yet they took opposite sides on conscription. Supporting the war effort did not mean backing conscription, so the option saying all helpers wanted it is wrong.
b.clue: Compare what the two women have in common and where they differ.

a.q: Which description of Australian women's part in the First World War is accurate?
opts: They nursed and knitted, and split over conscription
They fought as soldiers and led the home campaigns
They stayed out of the war effort and public debate
They knitted and nursed, and all backed conscription
a.why: Women nursed overseas, knitted and packed supplies at home, and joined the conscription debate on both sides. The option saying they all backed conscription is wrong because some women campaigned against it.

b.q: In 1917, Edith in Adelaide knits socks for soldiers and speaks out against conscription. Her neighbour Joan packs parcels for soldiers and speaks out for it. What does their story show about war work and views on conscription?
opts: Doing war work did not settle a woman's view
Doing war work meant a woman backed conscription
Doing war work meant a woman opposed conscription
Doing war work kept women out of public debates

b.clue: Compare what the two women share and where they part ways.
